content: This report provides detailed recommendations for preventing and controlling infectious diseases in dental settings, as well as addressing health and safety concerns for dental healthcare personnel (DHCP). It updates and revises previous CDC guidelines, incorporates relevant infection-control measures from other CDC guidelines, and addresses new concerns not previously covered in dental infection control. The updates include the application of standard precautions instead of universal precautions, work restrictions for healthcare personnel infected with or exposed to infectious diseases, management of occupational exposures to bloodborne pathogens (including postexposure prophylaxis for hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and HIV), and the selection and use of devices designed to prevent sharps injuries. These recommendations are based on data from well-designed scientific studies wherever possible. However, due to limited research on certain infection risks and prevention measures in dental healthcare, some recommendations are based on theoretical rationale, suggestive evidence, or expert opinion. In the United States, approximately 9 million individuals work in healthcare professions, including 168,000 dentists, 112,000 registered dental hygienists, 218,000 dental assistants, and 53,000 dental laboratory technicians. DHCP refers to all paid and unpaid personnel in dental settings who may be exposed to infectious materials, including body substances, contaminated supplies, equipment, environmental surfaces, water, or air. This includes clinical and non-clinical staff such as administrative, clerical, housekeeping, maintenance, or volunteer personnel. The guidelines aim to prevent disease transmission from patients to DHCP, from DHCP to patients, and between patients. While the focus is on outpatient, ambulatory dental settings, the recommended infection-control practices are applicable to all settings where dental treatment is provided. Both dental patients and DHCP can be exposed to pathogenic microorganisms, including cytomegalovirus, hepatitis B and C viruses, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, HIV, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, staphylococci, streptococci, and other oral and respiratory tract bacteria and viruses. Transmission can occur through direct contact with blood, oral fluids, or contaminated instruments, as well as through indirect contact with contaminated surfaces, droplet exposure, or inhalation of airborne microorganisms. Effective infection-control strategies interrupt the chain of infection by breaking one or more links in the transmission process. Previous CDC recommendations for dentistry primarily focused on reducing the risk of bloodborne pathogen transmission through universal precautions, which treated all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious. In 1996, the CDC expanded this concept to standard precautions, which integrate and expand universal precautions to include protection against pathogens spread by blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin, and mucous membranes. Saliva has always been considered potentially infectious in dental infection control, so there is no operational difference between universal and standard precautions in clinical dental practice. Standard precautions also address the prevention of transmission of diseases spread by contact, droplet, or airborne routes. Although patients with acute illnesses caused by these diseases typically do not seek routine dental care, DHCP must understand precautions for all transmission routes because they may encounter such patients in urgent care settings or become infected themselves. Dental practices should develop written infection-control programs to prevent or reduce the risk of disease transmission. These programs should include policies, procedures, and practices to prevent work-related injuries and illnesses among DHCP and healthcare-associated infections among patients. The program should reflect current scientific knowledge, adhere to relevant regulations, and be evaluated regularly to ensure its effectiveness. A designated infection-control coordinator should oversee the program, but maintaining a safe work environment requires the commitment of all DHCP. Education and training are critical for ensuring compliance with infection-control programs. DHCP should receive training on initial assignment, when new tasks or procedures affect their exposure risk, and at least annually. Training should cover exposure risks, prevention strategies, infection-control policies, and management of work-related illnesses and injuries, including postexposure prophylaxis. Educational materials should be appropriate for the audience's literacy and language levels and consistent with existing regulations. Immunization programs are essential for reducing the risk of infectious disease transmission among DHCP and patients. Vaccinations should be provided before DHCP are placed at risk of exposure. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends that all healthcare personnel, including DHCP, be vaccinated against hepatitis B, influenza, measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella. Employers are required to offer hepatitis B vaccination to employees with potential exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials (OPIM) and to follow CDC recommendations for vaccination and follow-up procedures. Exposure prevention and postexposure management are critical components of infection control. Standard precautions, engineering controls, work practices, and administrative controls should be used to minimize occupational exposures. Written policies should facilitate prompt reporting, evaluation, counseling, treatment, and follow-up of occupational exposures. DHCP should also be screened for tuberculosis (TB) at the beginning of employment and periodically based on the facility's TB risk level. DHCP with acute or chronic medical conditions that increase their susceptibility to opportunistic infections should consult with their healthcare providers to determine whether they can safely perform their duties.
